**Trade body warns digital euro could lock out open banking providers**

*The European Third Party Providers Association has called on EU policymakers to guarantee that payment initiation providers can access digital euro accounts, arguing current proposals risk undermining open banking principles.*

The ETPPA's intervention targets what it sees as a structural flaw in the emerging digital euro legislative framework: the potential exclusion of licensed payment initiation service providers from digital euro accounts. If enacted as currently drafted, the association argues, the digital euro would create a retail payment instrument that sits outside the open, non-discriminatory access regime established under PSD2 and carried forward into PSD3.

The concern is not abstract. PISPs have built business models on the right to initiate payments from customer accounts held at banks. A digital euro account without equivalent access rights would fragment the regulatory landscape, creating a two-tier system where some payment accounts are open and others are not. The ETPPA is pushing for explicit legislative language ensuring open banking obligations apply to digital euro accounts.

The timing matters. The digital euro regulation is moving through the EU legislative process alongside PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation, and the interaction between these frameworks will define how Europe's retail payments infrastructure works for the next decade. If the digital euro is carved out from third-party access rules, it would represent a significant policy reversal at a point when the EU is otherwise deepening its commitment to open finance.

*Sources: [ETPPA warns that digital euro proposals could undermine open banking](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110107/etppa-warns-that-digital-euro-proposals-could-undermine-open-banking) — Finextra*

**UKPI launches recurring payments scheme to scale commercial VRPs**

*The UK Payments Initiative has published its new open banking recurring payments scheme, establishing an industry-led framework for commercial variable recurring payments beyond the original sweeping mandate.*

UKPI's scheme provides the rulebook and operational standards needed to move commercial variable recurring payments from pilot to production. Until now, VRPs have been limited in practice to sweeping use cases — moving money between a customer's own accounts. The new scheme creates the governance layer for broader commercial applications such as subscription billing, utility payments and merchant-initiated collections.

The launch follows the FCA's open finance roadmap and the National Payments Vision, both of which identified account-to-account recurring payments as a priority. The scheme addresses a chicken-and-egg problem: banks have been reluctant to invest in VRP infrastructure without clear commercial rules, while fintechs and merchants have struggled to build propositions without reliable bank participation. An industry-endorsed scheme lowers the coordination cost on both sides.

Whether this translates into meaningful volume depends on bank adoption. The UK's major banks control the vast majority of current accounts, and their willingness to implement the scheme's standards will determine how quickly commercial VRPs become a viable alternative to card-on-file and direct debit for recurring payments.

*Sources: [UK Payments Initiative launches new open banking recurring payments scheme](https://www.lewissilkin.com/insights/2026/06/11/uk-payments-initiative-launches-new-open-banking-recurring-payments-scheme-102n1ql) — Lewis Silkin | [The A2A Paradigm Shift: How the UK's National Payments Vision Accelerates Commercial Open Banking](https://www.bobsguide.com/the-a2a-paradigm-shift-how-the-uks-national-payments-vision-accelerates-commercial-open-banking/) — Bobsguide*

**Devengo becomes first firm certified for cross-border SEPA instant payouts**

*Spanish payments firm Devengo has secured OCT Inst certification, enabling it to process cross-border instant payment payouts under the SEPA scheme — a capability that remains rare among non-bank providers.*

Devengo's certification for One-Leg Out Credit Transfer Instant (OCT Inst) allows it to process instant payouts that originate or terminate outside the SEPA zone, bridging euro instant payments with international corridors. The certification positions Devengo as an early mover in a space where most licensed providers are still limited to domestic or intra-SEPA instant transfers.

The development is relevant in the context of the EU's instant payments regulation, which mandates full SEPA instant reachability for euro-area banks by early 2027. As banks build out their instant payments infrastructure to meet the mandate, the adjacent opportunity is in cross-border flows where instant settlement intersects with payout use cases such as marketplace disbursements, gig economy payments and remittances. OCT Inst certification is the technical prerequisite for serving these corridors.

Devengo is a relatively small player, but the certification illustrates how the regulatory push toward instant payments is creating new infrastructure roles for specialist firms. The question is whether non-bank providers can capture meaningful share of cross-border instant flows before incumbent banks and networks extend their own capabilities.

*Sources: [Devengo premieres OCT Inst certification for global payments](https://www.democrata.es/en/economy/devengo-achieves-green-light-to-operate-cross-border-instant-payments-with-european-standard/amp/) — Demócrata*

**SEPA instant payments mandate forces rethink of bank liquidity management**

*As SEPA instant payment volumes scale ahead of the 2027 mandate, banks face growing pressure on intraday liquidity buffers and back-office processes built for batch settlement.*

The operational challenge of instant payments is shifting from connectivity to liquidity. A Finextra analysis by Fergus McKie argues that banks' existing liquidity management frameworks, designed around batch processing windows and predictable settlement cycles, are structurally misaligned with the demands of 24/7 real-time settlement. The result is that banks must either hold significantly larger liquidity buffers or invest in real-time cash position monitoring — both of which carry cost.

This is not a new observation, but it is becoming more urgent. The instant payments regulation requires euro-area banks to be fully reachable for SEPA instant credit transfers, and volumes are climbing as early adopters scale. Banks that treated instant payments as a low-volume overlay are discovering that rising transaction counts compound liquidity strain, particularly outside business hours when treasury desks are unstaffed and central bank facilities may be unavailable.

The back-office dimension is equally pressing. Reconciliation, fraud screening and sanctions checking all need to operate in real time to match front-end settlement speeds. Banks that have not automated these functions face a widening gap between the speed at which money moves and the speed at which they can confirm it moved correctly.

*Sources: [Real-time risk: SEPA Instant Payments is rewriting liquidity management](https://www.finextra.com/blogposting/31990/real-time-risk-sepa-instant-payments-is-rewriting-liquidity-management) — Finextra*
